analysis.one_liner: Forces agencies to periodically re-justify major federal regulations or terminate them.
analysis.headline: The Regulatory Sunset and Review Act of 2013, backed by 62 Republican cosponsors, never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made federal agencies periodically re-examine their biggest rules — generally those costing the economy $100 million a year or more — and either keep, change, combine, or kill them. A rule could only survive review if it met all the legal requirements that would apply to a brand-new rule, including cost-benefit and risk analysis. Businesses and others adversely affected by a rule could petition to have it reviewed, agencies would have to answer within 90 days, and decisions could be challenged in court. The White House regulatory office would have run the whole process, setting priorities and deadlines.
analysis.who_benefits: Regulated industries would have gained the most: any business adversely affected by a federal rule could petition to have it reviewed, and every major rule would periodically come up for re-justification under fresh cost-benefit standards — giving companies repeated chances to argue for weaker or terminated rules. Taxpayers might also have benefited where rules were genuinely obsolete or duplicative. People who rely on federal protections (for clean air, safe workplaces, safe products, or fair financial markets) would have gained only where review genuinely improved a rule, and carried the risk of losing protections they never asked to revisit.

how_it_helps.text: Agencies would have to review their most economically significant rules — those with $100 million or more in annual economic effects — every three to seven years, and modify, consolidate, or terminate those that prove obsolete, duplicative, or unjustified.

Any person adversely affected by a smaller rule could petition for its review, the agency would have to answer within 90 days (with limited extensions), a public log of petitions would be kept, and denials or delays could be challenged in court.

Congressional committees, or a majority of their members from either party, could request sunset review of rules below the $100 million threshold, giving lawmakers a tool to target specific regulations.
Related rules would be grouped for simultaneous review, with priority given to those imposing the greatest costs, so overlapping requirements across agencies could be cleaned up together.

analysis.who_pays: Federal agencies would have borne the cost: an inventory of every significant rule, staggered review deadlines, a designated Regulatory Review Officer at each agency, and full new-rulemaking analysis to keep existing rules. The public would have paid where review weakened or delayed protections — if a rule were terminated, deadlines tied to it would be suspended until a replacement rule was issued.
analysis.who_pays_short: Agencies, and the public where protections weaken

drawbacks.text: Any rule continued after review would have to meet all the legal requirements that apply to a brand-new rule, including cost-benefit and standardized risk analysis — meaning long-standing protections for health, safety, and the environment would have to be re-justified from scratch on a recurring cycle, reopening settled questions.

The petition process is open only to people adversely affected by a rule — in practice, regulated businesses — while the people who benefit from a rule (through cleaner air, safer products, or financial protections) have no equivalent fast track, so the review machinery is oriented toward the regulated side.

If a covered rule is terminated, deadlines that depend on it are suspended until the agency issues a new rule on the same subject, which could leave obligations and protections in limbo during the gap.

The bill would create substantial new machinery — a governmentwide rule inventory, staggered review lists, a Regulatory Review Officer at every agency, and multi-stage notices and reports — diverting agency resources from writing and enforcing rules in the first place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The appeal is real: agencies accumulate rules that outlive their purpose, and a structured review with public petitions and deadlines could catch them. But the design tilts the process toward regulated parties — only people "adversely affected" by a rule can petition, and any rule kept on the books must clear the full legal hurdles of a brand-new rule, including fresh cost-benefit and risk analysis. That would effectively put every major protection up for periodic re-litigation, and if a rule were terminated, related deadlines would pause until a replacement issued. A lighter-touch lookback limited to genuinely obsolete rules might have captured most of the benefit at far less risk; this version did not strike that balance.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees and then a Judiciary subcommittee for nearly two years without a hearing or vote, and expired when the 113th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Randy Hultgren introduced the bill on January 18, 2013, with the stated purpose of requiring agencies to regularly review significant rules and terminate those that are obsolete, unnecessary, or duplicative.
The same day, the House referred it to two committees — Oversight and Government Reform and the Judiciary — a dual referral that requires both panels to act before the bill can advance.

On February 28, 2013, the Judiciary Committee referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law. Neither the full committees nor the subcommittee took it up again.
No further action appears in the record before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, so the bill never reached the House floor or the Senate and died automatically.
All 62 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on.

Had it passed, every significant rule — those with $100 million or more in annual economic effects — would have faced a mandatory review deadline, and a rule could only continue in effect if it met all the legal requirements for a newly issued rule, including cost-benefit and risk analysis.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Existing federal rules stayed on the books unchanged, and the agencies that issued them avoided a new cycle of re-justification; regulated industries did not get the review-and-termination tool the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies and the rules already on the books

industries.industry: Regulated industries (manufacturing, energy, finance, and other businesses subject to major federal rules)
industries.note: The bill would have created a recurring pathway to reopen, consolidate, or terminate the major rules that govern them, with petitions available to adversely affected parties and strict court deadlines on agency responses. It died in committee, so nothing changed. For ordinary people, the same tool that removes obsolete red tape also risks dismantling protections they rely on.

Agencies would have taken on a standing obligation to inventory, re-justify, and re-analyze their significant rules — including meeting the full legal requirements of a new rulemaking to keep a rule — with a designated Regulatory Review Officer at each agency answering to the White House regulatory office. Their interest in keeping existing rules runs alongside the public's interest in the protections those rules deliver.

industries.industry: Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (the White House regulatory office)
industries.note: The office would have gained centralized power over which rules are reviewed, in what order, and on what timetable governmentwide. Its stake is procedural rather than financial, so how that power cuts for or against the public would depend on who held the office.
